a sign-out; the request's step, which receives the admitted session.
judgement.why: The later contracts define one route per OwnerAction, derive its method and path, identify changes through their CSRF-bearing forms, and enumerate the upload-touching request classes.

topics.topic: Exact query-parameter, CSRF form-field, and session-cookie names
questions: What exact query-parameter name does `OWNER_TARGET_PARAMETER` contain?
What exact form-field name does `OWNER_CSRF_FIELD` contain for ordinary and multipart forms?
What exact cookie name does `OWNER_SESSION_COOKIE_NAME` contain?
What exact query-parameter, form-field and cookie names do these three constants contain?

quotes:
The target is the query parameter
  `OWNER_TARGET_PARAMETER` (`target`) names, an identity and never a
  personal value (R0-29).

The CSRF value is the field
  `OWNER_CSRF_FIELD` (`csrf`) names, the upload's first part included, and
  `OwnerRequest.csrf_value` carries it from the form's reading to the
  request's admission, since a body is read once.

The session cookie is
  named `OWNER_SESSION_COOKIE_NAME` (`__Host-registry_session`): set
  `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `Path=/` and no `Domain`, which the `__Host-` prefix
  makes a browser require (A13 rule 1), and `SameSite=Strict`, so a browser
  never sends it with a request another site started (owner, 2026-11-24;
  OWASP).
judgement.why: State 6 fixes the three literal names as target, csrf, and __Host-registry_session.

topics.topic: Request facts preserved after an owner-request parsing failure
questions: Which already-read parts survive when a body, upload head, or form cannot be read: the matched action, target, session cookie and other headers, or none of them?

When parsing fails, which successfully read request facts survive in `OwnerRequest` or `OwnerAdmission`: the method/path-derived action, session cookie, target query parameter, CSRF value, and any complete form fields read before the failure?

quotes:
A request whose body, upload head or
form cannot be read is handed on with no values, no CSRF value and no
credential, nothing partly read kept: it is admitted or refused by the
ordinary checks, a change refused at stage (1) for its missing CSRF value,
a sign-in as a missing credential (owner, 2026-11-24; option (a) of the
question State 4 round-51 and round-55 T3 carried to State 7).
judgement.why: The later surface contract preserves the route and session admission facts while clearing body-derived values, the CSRF value, and the sign-in credential, so ordinary session admission still occurs.

topics.topic: Classification of OWNER_ACTIONS rows as changes requiring CSRF checks
questions: Which OwnerAction rows are changes, and what invariant makes this flag agree with A13's requirement that every owner-interface change undergo the session's CSRF check?

quotes:
An owner
  action is addressed by its row of the data provider's `OWNER_ACTIONS`
  (row model `OwnerActionRoute`, one row per `OwnerAction` member): a read
  by `GET`, every other action by `POST`, at the path `/` and the action's
  value, the project list at `/`; the row also says whether the action is a
  change, whose form carries the CSRF value (A13 rule 2), and whether it
  touches an uploaded file (A16 rule 2) — `show_confirmation` touching one
  only when its `confirm_action` is `confirm_import`.

A link or a form addresses its action by that action's row of
`OWNER_ACTIONS` and its target by `OWNER_TARGET_PARAMETER`; a read is a
link or a GET form, which carries no CSRF value, and every change a POST
form carrying it, so no secret is ever in a URL (R0-29).
judgement.why: The later contract makes reads GET requests without CSRF and every change a POST form carrying CSRF, fixing the invariant that the route's change flag must represent state-changing actions.

topics.topic: Delegation path from owner requests through operations to domain capabilities
questions: For each owner-facing form, read, list, mapping, confirmation-step and newest-backup request, does `serve_owner_request` call `capability:operations.perform_owner_operation`, and which operation then calls the named domain capability and supplies the admission or refusal answer?
When the next body bytes do not arrive before the listener timeout, must Registry close the connection unanswered or create an empty-valued request and return an operation answer?

judgement.why: This is the same read-timeout failure-outcome, response, and connection-cleanup question already judged non-blocking in P3, and the relevant passages have not changed.

precedent.topic: Read-timeout failure outcome, response, diagnostics, and upload cleanup
quotes:
`instance_lifecycle`'s two listeners share one HTTP implementation. Each
connection's socket waits at most the imported
`LISTENER_READ_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (30) for the next bytes of a request — its
headers or its body, an upload's head and file among them; a wait that
reaches it ends the stream with a failure, which the reader sees as any
stream failure: an upload's head then gives no CSRF value (refused at stage
(1)), its file part `file_unreadable`, and the connection is closed. A
request answered before its body was read to its framed end — any request,
not an upload alone — has the remainder discarded unread and its
connection closed; a connection carries a next request only after one whose
body was read to its end.

No refusal
carries a digest: a file over the size limit is refused before any of it is
parsed — a declared length over it before any byte is read, otherwise as
soon as more than it has been read; a stream that fails or ends before its
declared length is refused as `file_unreadable`, replacing nothing kept and
changing nothing of the session but the instant of its last request, which
every request carrying it moves (A13 rule 2) — and an
unreadable or malformed one is refused with its kind alone.

After an upload's answer, whatever it was — accepted, or refused before any
or after some bytes were read — `owner_interface` discards the unread
remainder of the body without reading it into anything and closes the
connection its listener accepted; a connection that carried an upload is
never reused.
precedent.why: State 6 makes timeout expiry a stream failure: during the head it yields a stage-(1) refusal, during the file it yields `file_unreadable` without replacing the kept upload, and the upload connection is then closed after unread-body cleanup.

topics.topic: Propagation and lock-order behavior for the uploaded-file flag
questions: Which module and capability consume this flag, pass it across the owner-interface boundary, and acquire the import lock before the session lock for every affected request?

quotes:
The session identity from the cookie, or none; whether the request is a
change; the CSRF value it carries, for a change; whether it reads or
changes an uploaded file — an upload, the mapping, the import's
confirmation step, a confirmation, a sign-out, change or not; whether it is
a sign-out; the request's step, which receives the admitted session.

The step runs holding the session's
lock when the request is a change or touches an uploaded file, and for the
latter the import lock taken before it; both are released when the step
returns, on every path (Conventions, "Locks of an owner request").

After the check, a change that touches no uploaded file takes its
place on the session's lock at once; a request that touches one first waits
for the import lock and then takes its place, so the locks are always taken
import first and no place on a session's lock waits for the import lock (A16
rule 2).
judgement.why: The later API makes operations pass the upload-touching fact to owner_sessions.admit_owner_request, which takes the import lock before the session lock and runs the step under both.

topics.topic: Target identifier and form-value identifiers for each owner action
questions: For each owner action, which identifier is its target, especially actions naming multiple records such as granting a project to a session, and which other identifiers belong in form values?

quotes:
The action is the row of the imported `OWNER_ACTIONS` constant whose method
and path are the request's, and that row says whether the request is a
change and whether it touches an uploaded file — the confirmation step
touching one only when the action it confirms is the import; the target is
the query parameter the imported `OWNER_TARGET_PARAMETER` constant names;
the CSRF value is the form field the imported `OWNER_CSRF_FIELD` constant
names; the session is the cookie the imported `OWNER_SESSION_COOKIE_NAME`
constant names (owner, 2026-11-24).
judgement.why: Assigning each action's identifiers to the shared target parameter or typed form fields is a request encoding and contract question owned by State 6, not a missing State 4 owner, outcome, or capability.

topics.topic: Uniqueness and conflict handling for OWNER_ACTIONS routes
questions: Must method-and-path pairs be unique, and what happens if two rows match the same request?

quotes:
An owner
  action is addressed by its row of the data provider's `OWNER_ACTIONS`
  (row model `OwnerActionRoute`, one row per `OwnerAction` member): a read
  by `GET`, every other action by `POST`, at the path `/` and the action's
  value, the project list at `/`; the row also says whether the action is a
  change, whose form carries the CSRF value (A13 rule 2), and whether it
  touches an uploaded file (A16 rule 2) — `show_confirmation` touching one
  only when its `confirm_action` is `confirm_import`.
judgement.why: State 6 defines exactly one row for each OwnerAction and derives each non-list route from that action's distinct value, leaving no first-match or ambiguous-match behavior to choose.
